newsitem.title: ITALY: Mediobanca, BCI seen as partners despite denial.
newsitem.headline: Mediobanca, BCI seen as partners despite denial.

text.p: A tie-up between merchant bank Mediobanca and retail bank Banca Commerciale Italiana would be a match made in heaven, analysts believe, but both parties hotly deny they are in pursuit of each other.

Shares in both banks shot up on the Milan bourse after La Repubblica newspaper reported on Monday that Mediobanca, Italy's top merchant bank, and BCI, popularly known as Comit, were finalising a full-blown merger plan.
"All that is missing is the go-ahead and within a few weeks everything could be signed and sealed," said the report by Sergio Turani, the newspaper's most influential columnist.

Mediobanca shares leaped 8.78 percent and Comit jumped 6.77 percent on Monday and Tuesday but then went into reverse on Wednesday after the banks issued a joint statement saying the Repubblica report was groundless.

The report of a merger between Comit and Mediobanca broke at a time when the rumour mill in Italy's banking world is at fever pitch with reports flying thick and fast that some of the giants of the sector are pairing off with each other.
Italy's biggest savings bank Cariplo is reported to be in talks with Banco Ambrosiano Veneto on a possible link-up while IMI is said to be discussing an alliance with Turin's San Paolo.
Of all the rumoured tie-ups, a merger between Mediobanca and Comit is the one that has set pulses racing in Milan's close-knit financial community.

"It makes a lot of sense because Mediobanca and Banca Commerciale are perfectly complementary," said a London-based analyst with a major investment bank. "With all this talk of other banks tying up with each other Comit has to do something."

Both banks, which have links going back many years and already own shareholdings in each other, are coming under pressure in a fast-changing environment as competition hots up at home in a banking market that is opening up.

Mediobanca, which has been Italy's foremost corporate deal-maker, suffered an unprecedented humiliation in 1995 when its plan to create a super-conglomerate with chemicals group Montedison at its core had to be abandoned.

The episode was seen as a stinging reverse for Enrico Cuccia, Mediobanca's 90-year-old honorary chairman who set up the bank after World War Two and carved out a role as a power broker between Italy's powerful business families.
Cuccia is believed to be anxious to find a partner to help to bolster Mediobanca's balance sheet.

The bank, which owns a clutch of strategic stakes in Italy's top blue chip companies, had to drop plans for a rights issue in June 1994 aimed at raising between 1.5 and 1.9 trillion lire ($880 million and $1.1 billion) after share prices plunged.

Analysts say a tie-up with BCI, which has a network of overseas offices, would give Mediobanca an international dimension as well as creating a group with strong retail and investment banking interests.

Comit, which was privatised in 1994, has failed to act decisively since an attempt to take over Ambroveneto was warded off two years ago. Its share price, languishing at around 3,500 lire, has sunk to well below its 5,400 lire offer price of three years ago.

Whether or not it does make it to the altar with Mediobanca, Comit has to tackle problems of chronic over-staffing and inefficiency faced by most of Italy's large retail banks if it it is find favour again among investors.

"The big retail banks such as Banca Commerciale are going to be the big losers if they do not go about restructuring their businesses very soon," said a banking analyst with a Milan finance house. ($ = 1699 Italian Lire)
